title: The Main Ridge — Running the Krkonoše Border Path

bestPeriod.note: Several ridge and glacial-cirque paths are legally closed 1 November to 31 May for grouse and vegetation; June is open, empty and still cold up top.

summary: Seven days on the Czech-Polish crest of the Krkonoše, from the Elbe source to Sněžka, using the boudy as water stops and the chairlifts as escape routes.
hook: The Krkonoše look modest on paper — nothing tops 1,603 m — and then you get on the crest and find arctic-alpine tundra, dwarf pine, and a wind that has come off the North European Plain with nothing in its way. This is a subtle, weather-driven range with a superb hut network and a marking system so good you can navigate it by colour alone. Run it as a ridge week: the boudy are your aid stations, the valleys are your recovery, and Sněžka waits until Friday.

snapshot.Base(s): Špindlerův Mlýn (4 nights), Pec pod Sněžkou (3 nights)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 120–140 km, 5,000–5,800 m vert; granite paving, tundra path, forest track, boardwalk
snapshot.Getting There: Prague (PRG) → direct coach to Špindlerův Mlýn (approx. 2h45), or train to Vrchlabí and bus
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners who like long exposed days, cold wind and cheap hut soup

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Svatý Petr valley
itinerary.morning: Coach from Prague's Černý Most or Florenc terminal to Špindlerův Mlýn. Buy a bus ticket in advance online; the seats sell out on summer Fridays.
itinerary.afternoon: Shake the coach out of your legs. Run up the Svatý Petr valley on the green-marked path toward Pláň, turn at the top of the piste, and come back down the Labe riverside path through town. Nothing above threshold.
itinerary.evening: Learn the Czech marking system before you need it: 10 cm painted stripes, a coloured band between two white ones, red for the main ridge, then blue, green and yellow for connectors. Junction posts carry timings in hours, not kilometres.
itinerary.dayStats: 11 km, 400 m vert. Grade T1, forest track and gravel road, no exposure. Water: Špindlerův Mlýn taps and shops; the Labe here is not drinking water. Bail-out: you are never more than 20 min from town.

itinerary.title: Western crest: Zlaté návrší, the Elbe source and the Sněžné jámy
itinerary.morning: Take the Medvědín chairlift out of Špindlerův Mlýn to 1,235 m — this is the cheap 600 m of the week, use it. Run west along the red-marked ridge over Zlaté návrší to Labská bouda (1,340 m), perched above the Labský důl cirque.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue north on the border path past Pramen Labe, the ceremonial source of the Elbe, then up over Vysoké Kolo (1,509 m) and along the rim of the Sněžné jámy — two deep glacial cirques falling away on the Polish side, and the most dramatic drop in the range. Return via Vosecká bouda and Martinova bouda, then descend the blue trail to Špindlerův Mlýn.
itinerary.evening: Eat at one of the town's pubs. Kulajda, svíčková, dumplings, a large mineral water.
itinerary.dayStats: 26 km, 950 m vert (lift-assisted), 1,450 m descent. Grade T2, granite slab paving and tundra path; serious wind exposure on the crest, vertical drops on the cirque rims — stay behind the barriers. Water: Labská bouda, Vosecká bouda, Martinova bouda. Bail-out: Horní Mísečky road at Zlaté návrší; the Medvědín chairlift.

itinerary.title: Recovery in the Labský důl
itinerary.morning: Easy and low. Run the valley path from Špindlerův Mlýn up the Labe to the Labský vodopád viewpoint below Labská bouda, on shaded forest road with a gentle constant gradient.
itinerary.afternoon: Turn around before the steep zig-zags. Total 70 minutes at conversational pace. Spend the afternoon flat — the town has a heated outdoor pool and several hotel saunas that sell day access.
itinerary.evening: Check the forecast for the week's two big days. The Krkonoše ridge is the windiest place in Czechia and gusts routinely make running the crest pointless.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 350 m vert. Grade T1, forest road. Water: Špindlerův Mlýn. Bail-out: the valley road runs the whole way.

itinerary.title: Climb session to Luční bouda by the Bílé Labe
itinerary.morning: The quality day. From Špindlerův Mlýn follow the Bílé Labe (White Elbe) valley east on the Weberova cesta — a rocky, rooty, cascade-lined path that is one of the prettiest lines in the park — then take the steep climb up to Luční bouda (1,410 m), the enormous inter-war hut on the Bílá louka plateau.
itinerary.afternoon: Soup and refill at Luční bouda, then descend to Špindlerova bouda on the ridge and drop the blue trail home. Treat the climb as one sustained tempo effort and the rest of the day as easy.
itinerary.dayStats: 22 km, 900 m vert. Grade T2 with short T3 rock steps in the Bílé Labe gorge; wet granite, roots, no fall exposure. Water: Bouda u Bílého Labe (seasonal), Luční bouda, Špindlerova bouda. Bail-out: the Bílé Labe path exits back to town at any point; the Špindlerova bouda road has a bus stop.

itinerary.title: Transfer to Pec pod Sněžkou, easy legs in the Obří důl
itinerary.morning: Bus over the ridge road via Vrchlabí or the direct seasonal connection to Pec pod Sněžkou. Drop bags.
itinerary.afternoon: A short, easy reconnaissance of tomorrow's start: run the blue path up the Obří důl — the great glacial trench under the south face of Sněžka — as far as the Kaplička and the old mine adits, then turn back. Look up. That headwall is the last climb of Day 6.
itinerary.evening: Early food in Pec. Buy tomorrow's supplies; the shops here shut by 19:00.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km, 400 m vert. Grade T1–T2, gravel service road and stony path. Water: Pec pod Sněžkou taps; Obří důl streams are clean but untreated. Bail-out: single valley, one road, trivial.

itinerary.title: Sněžka and the Path of Czech-Polish Friendship
itinerary.morning: Out at first light. Climb the Obří důl to the Obří sedlo, then the final rocky steps to Sněžka (1,603 m) — the highest point in Czechia, with the baroque Chapel of St Lawrence, the Czech post office building and, forty metres below on the Polish side, the Dom Śląski refuge.
itinerary.afternoon: Head west on the Cesta česko-polského přátelství, the Path of Czech-Polish Friendship, which runs the border crest with markers on both sides. Over Svorová hora, past Slezský dům, across the Bílá louka to Luční bouda, then Studniční hora's flank and down to Výrovka (1,370 m). Descend the Zelený důl to Pec.
itinerary.evening: This is the day of the week. Eat, drink, do not set an alarm.
itinerary.dayStats: 29 km, 1,500 m vert, 1,500 m descent. Grade T2–T3; the Obří důl headwall is steep rock steps with chains in places, the crest is paved granite and tundra with total wind exposure and no shelter for 8 km. Water: Dom Śląski and the Sněžka summit buildings, Luční bouda, Výrovka. Bail-out: the Sněžka cable car from the summit down via Růžová hora to Pec; from the crest, the Luční bouda–Pec valley path.

itinerary.title: Růžová hora at dawn, then out
itinerary.morning: Ride the first cable-car section from Pec to Růžová hora (1,390 m), watch the light come onto Sněžka's cone, and run the ridge path down through the dwarf pine to Pec — 500 m of gentle, forgiving descent.
itinerary.afternoon: Coffee, shower, coach back to Prague from Pec pod Sněžkou.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km, 100 m vert, 550 m descent. Grade T2, stone path and boardwalk. Water: Růžová hora buffet, Pec. Bail-out: the cable car runs both directions.

accommodationStrategy.name: Pensions on the Labe in Špindlerův Mlýn
accommodationStrategy.description: Špindlerův Mlýn is a purpose-built mountain town, which means abundant, cheap, unglamorous pensions with drying rooms and half-board — exactly what a running week needs. Take one within walking distance of the Medvědín chairlift base so you are not adding a bus leg to every morning. Half-board is worth taking: the kitchen opens for breakfast before the lifts.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6 weeks ahead for July–August; longer for weekends.

accommodationStrategy.name: Luční bouda
accommodationStrategy.description: The largest and oldest of the ridge boudy, sitting where the two big traverses cross. Worth one night mid-week if you want to start Day 6 already on the plateau and watch the sunrise on the Bílá louka rather than climbing to it. It has proper beds, a restaurant, and it is the single most useful water point in the range.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 8–10 weeks ahead in summer; it fills fast.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €35–€60 per person in a shared room

accommodationStrategy.name: Pensions in Pec pod Sněžkou
accommodationStrategy.description: Pec is smaller and quieter than Špindlerův Mlýn and sits directly under the Obří důl and the Sněžka cable car, which puts the two escape options and the biggest day's trailhead on your doorstep. Ask about parking if you drive — the village restricts vehicle access to the upper valley.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European. Czech mountain rescue is Horská služba, reachable on **1210** — save it; they run stations at Špindlerův Mlýn, Pec pod Sněžkou and Luční bouda.
logistics.weather: You will cross into Poland repeatedly on the crest path, which is normal and requires nothing. Carry ID anyway. Polish huts price in złoty; most take cards.
logistics.money: Czechia uses the koruna. Cards are near-universal, including in most boudy, but carry 500–1,000 CZK for the smaller huts and the Polish side. Refuse dynamic currency conversion at card terminals.
logistics.transportRules: Direct coaches run Prague–Špindlerův Mlýn and Prague–Pec pod Sněžkou daily; book online in advance for a reserved seat. Within the park, seasonal shuttle buses connect the valleys and the ridge road.

other.label: You must stay on marked trails
other.text: Krkonoše is a national park with strict zoning; leaving the marked path in the first zone is an offence and is enforced by rangers on the ridge. This is not a place for improvised lines.

other.label: Seasonal closures are legal, not advisory
other.text: A number of ridge and cirque trails close from 1 November to 31 May. Some paths also close temporarily for grouse breeding. Signs are in Czech, Polish, German and English.

other.label: Wind is the primary hazard
other.text: Sněžka records some of the strongest sustained winds in Central Europe. If the summit forecast shows gusts above 70 km/h, the crest is not runnable — swap to a valley day.

other.label: Opening hours
other.text: Village shops close around 18:00–19:00 and many close Sunday afternoon. Huts serve food all day but stop hot dishes earlier than you expect at altitude.

other.label: Camping, fires and drones
other.text: All prohibited within the national park. Bivouacking is not tolerated.

proTips: Ride the Medvědín chairlift up and run the crest west-to-east. You buy 600 m of altitude for the price of a coffee, and the prevailing wind then pushes you along the ridge instead of into your face.

Climb Sněžka from the Obří důl on the Czech side and descend the Path of Czech-Polish Friendship. The Polish approach from Karpacz carries most of the summit traffic; the Obří důl is steeper, wilder and quieter before 09:00.
Time the summit for before 09:00 or after 16:00. Between those hours Sněžka is one of the busiest mountaintops in Europe and the summit path becomes a single-file queue.

Use the junction post timings as a pacing tool. Czech signs give walking hours; a fit trail runner covers them at roughly 0.4–0.5 of the posted time on the flat crest and far closer to 1.0 on the rocky descents.
Luční bouda is open all year and is the only reliable water on the Bílá louka. Fill both flasks there even if you feel fine — the plateau has no springs and the tundra streams are peaty.
Buy the Sněžka cable-car ticket as a single up, not a return, and only on the day. Weather stops it regularly and the queue at Pec is worst between 10:00 and 12:00.
Špindlerův Mlýn's outdoor pool and the hotel saunas sell day passes cheaply. On a five-figure-descent week, that is the highest-value €10 you will spend.

packingNotes: Shoes with firm, moderately lugged outsoles. The crest is paved with granite slabs and quartzite blocks; soft mud shoes are wasted and the rock chews soft foam.
A proper windproof jacket, not a rain shell. Wind, not rain, is what stops days here.
Gloves and a beanie, June through September, without exception.
Long tights or leg covers for the Bílé Labe gorge and the dwarf-pine sections, which scratch.
1 L carrying capacity is enough given the hut density, plus a collapsible cup for spring taps.
A small amount of Czech cash and a card that does not charge for foreign transactions.
Offline maps plus the KČT colour logic: red = main ridge, and every junction post names the next two destinations with times.
Sunglasses and sunscreen — the plateau is treeless tundra and reflects hard even under cloud.
Trekking poles for the Obří důl headwall and the Zelený důl descent.
A dry bag for the Day 6 kit change; the crest and the valley can be 15°C apart.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Ridge-strength wind cancels Day 6.** Fallback: run the Bílé Labe and Modrý důl valleys from Pec, both sheltered and both offering 800 m of gain, and push Sněžka to Day 7 with the cable car as insurance.

**A trail you planned on is under seasonal closure.** Fallback: check the KRNAP closure map before the trip and again at your pension. The Path of Czech-Polish Friendship and the main valley routes are open in summer; the cirque descents are the ones that close.

**Fog on the Bílá louka.** The plateau is flat, featureless tundra and disorienting in cloud. Fallback: the crest is lined with tall wooden marker poles specifically for this — follow them, do not cut corners, and aim for Luční bouda, which is heated and open year-round.
**The Prague coach is sold out on your return day.** Fallback: local bus to Trutnov or Vrchlabí and a train onward; slower but frequent.

**Storms on the crest.** Convective storms build in July and August afternoons and there is no shelter for kilometres on the border path. Fallback: the boudy are spaced roughly an hour apart along the ridge — plan every crest day so you are never more than 30 minutes from one.
